families.s: HSE oxygen-enrichment, oxygen-deficiency and welding-gas guidance
families.t: oxygen fire risk, inert-gas asphyxiation, leak control, ventilation, atmosphere testing, cylinder handling and emergency precautions
f: Oxygen enrichment makes materials ignite more easily and burn more fiercely.
Inert and shielding gases can displace air and create an oxygen-deficient atmosphere without warning.
Many inert gases are odourless, so smell cannot be relied on to detect an unsafe atmosphere.
An enclosed or poorly ventilated area can allow leaked gases to accumulate.
An atmosphere must never be made safe by adding oxygen because this can greatly increase fire risk.
Gas work should control leaks, close cylinder valves and use suitable ventilation.
Where hazardous atmospheres are possible, assessment may require atmospheric measurement and emergency arrangements.
Oxygen, fuel gases and cylinders must be kept away from incompatible contamination, heat and physical damage.
families.g: Gas risk depends on gas type, leak rate, room volume, ventilation, oxygen concentration, ignition sources, cylinder and hose integrity, work duration and atmosphere monitoring.

families.s: HSE motor-vehicle-repair mechanical, lifting and occupational-health guidance
families.t: vehicle support, pits, machinery, oils, dusts, fumes, airbags, air conditioning, competence and workshop organisation
f: Many fatal motor-vehicle-repair incidents involve people being crushed beneath inadequately supported vehicles.
Raised vehicles must be supported using suitable equipment on stable ground before work begins.
Frequent or prolonged contact with used engine oil can cause dermatitis and other skin disease.
MVR risk control covers inspection pits, tyre work, exhausts, body repair, valeting, roadside recovery and workshop machinery.
Dusty body preparation should be separated from other work where practicable.
Powered sanding and discing should use built-in extraction or local exhaust ventilation.
Airbags, air conditioning and electric or hybrid vehicles introduce additional stored-energy and substance hazards.
Workers need suitable competence, information, equipment maintenance and supervision for the specific repair tasks.
families.g: MVR risk depends on vehicle type, lifting and support, stored energy, fuel and electrical systems, tools, pits, ventilation, hazardous substances, competence and workshop layout.

families.t: spray booths, clearance times, air-fed RPE, biological monitoring, asthma and dermatitis surveillance and booth maintenance
f: Isocyanate-containing two-pack paints can cause occupational asthma and dermatitis.
Exposure must be reduced as far below the applicable workplace exposure limit as reasonably practicable.
Spraying should be carried out in a properly extracted booth or room with a known clearance time.
Sprayers normally require suitable air-fed breathing apparatus rather than a particulate-filter mask.
Other suitable PPE is required to prevent skin and eye exposure.
Health surveillance is normally required for asthma and skin effects.
Biological monitoring can check whether exposure controls are working and HSE recommends regular monitoring for vehicle spray painters.
Booth airflow indicators, maintenance, examination, cleaning and observance of clearance time are essential to control.
families.g: Spray risk depends on paint chemistry, application method, booth airflow, clearance time, sprayer position, RPE air quality and fit, skin protection, cleaning, maintenance and exposure monitoring.

families.s: HSE electric and hybrid vehicle repair and recovery guidance
families.t: high voltage, stored energy, isolation, verification, battery damage, fire, manufacturer information and competent work
f: Electric and hybrid vehicles introduce hazards in addition to normal vehicle repair and recovery risks.
High-voltage systems can retain dangerous electrical energy even when the vehicle is switched off.
Work should follow manufacturer information and a suitable isolation procedure.
Isolation should prevent inadvertent reconnection and be verified before exposed high-voltage work.
Only people with appropriate training and competence should carry out work on high-voltage systems.
Damaged batteries can create electrical, chemical, thermal and fire risks.
Charging, roadside recovery and collision damage require controls specific to the vehicle and battery condition.
Work areas, tools, warning signs and access control should reflect the voltage and stored-energy hazards.
families.g: EV risk depends on system voltage, battery chemistry and state, collision damage, isolation design, stored charge, manufacturer procedure, tools, competence, charging and emergency response.

families.s: HSE tyre removal, wheel repair, inflation and hot-work guidance
families.t: competence, deflation, component inspection, restraint, remote inflation, explosion paths, multipiece wheels and heating hazards
f: Tyre and wheel repair and replacement should be performed by competent people.
Tyres should be fully deflated before removal, dismantling or relevant repair work.
Multipiece wheels can fail violently if components are damaged, mismatched or assembled incorrectly.
Inflation arrangements should keep the operator outside the likely explosion path.
A clip-on connector and sufficiently long airline can allow remote inflation from a safer position.
Suitable restraint, cage or other protective arrangement may be needed during inflation.
Heating a wheel rim with a tyre attached can cause a violent tyre explosion even when the tyre is deflated.
Wheel, rim, tyre and valve condition should be inspected and incompatible or damaged components removed from service.
families.g: Tyre risk depends on wheel type, pressure, component compatibility and damage, inflation method, restraint, operator position, heat, competence and manufacturer instructions.

families.s: HSE vehicle-exhaust-emission control in workshops and inspection pits
families.t: static running, tailpipe extraction, safe discharge, ventilation, pit exposure, maintenance and protection of nearby people
f: Vehicle exhaust emissions contain substances that can harm health.
Unnecessary static running of engines indoors should be avoided.
A scavenging system should be connected to the tailpipe during static running, particularly over an inspection pit.
Extracted exhaust should discharge to a safe outdoor location.
The discharge should not be drawn back into the workshop or affect nearby premises or people.
Inspection pits can increase exposure because exhaust gases may collect in low areas.
Workshop ventilation does not remove the need for effective source capture where engines run indoors.
Exhaust extraction, hoses, fans and connections should be maintained and checked for effective operation.
families.g: Exhaust risk depends on engine and fuel, running time, cold start, source capture, room and pit ventilation, discharge location, maintenance and the number of exposed people.

families.s: HSE bakery flour-dust and baker's-asthma control guidance
families.t: asthmagen control, low-dust flour, handling, extraction, WELs, enzymes, housekeeping, RPE and health surveillance
f: Flour dust is a recognised asthmagen and can cause occupational asthma and respiratory irritation.
Exposure should be reduced as far below the workplace exposure limit as reasonably practicable.
Flour dust has long-term and short-term WELs, but good practice aims substantially below those limits.
Low-dust flour can reduce airborne dust during sieving, tipping and surface dusting.
Careful handling, low-drop pouring and avoiding uncontrolled dust generation reduce exposure.
Enclosure and suitable dust extraction should be used for dust-generating processes where practicable.
Some bakery enzymes and improvers are potent respiratory sensitisers and should be supplied in less dusty forms where possible.
RPE and respiratory health surveillance may be required where residual inhalation risk remains.
families.g: Flour-dust risk depends on flour and additive type, dustiness, task, handling method, enclosure, extraction, housekeeping, duration, RPE and worker sensitisation.

families.s: HSE hairdressing dermatitis, asthma and hand-protection guidance
families.t: wet work, dyes, bleaches, sprays, glove choice, hand care, ventilation, skin checks and early symptom response
f: Hairdressing products and repeated wet work can cause irritant or allergic contact dermatitis.
Some hair sprays and other products can aggravate or cause respiratory symptoms.
Suitable gloves should be worn for shampooing and chemical treatments.
Powdered latex gloves should be avoided because latex can cause skin reactions and respiratory sensitisation.
Disposable nitrile or vinyl gloves may be suitable for many wet and chemical tasks.
Good hand care includes prompt decontamination, thorough drying and regular use of suitable moisturiser.
Regular skin checks can detect early dryness, redness, cracking or other dermatitis symptoms.
Mixing and using dyes, bleaches and sprays should minimise skin contact and inhalation and use suitable ventilation.
families.g: Hairdressing risk depends on product ingredients, wet-work duration, glove material and change frequency, aerosols, ventilation, hand-care practice, existing skin disease and sensitisation.
